questions.prompt: Which test strategy provides stronger evidence than a single passing happy-path example?
options: Mock every component so no integration is ever checked.
Test expected behavior, edge cases and failure paths, and add type-level tests for public type contracts where useful.
Only measure line coverage and assume that proves correctness.
questions.answer_key: Test expected behavior, edge cases and failure paths, and add type-level tests for public type contracts where useful.
questions.explanation: Coverage is a signal, not proof; test quality depends on assertions, cases and realistic boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “Type-Level Testing”?
options: The concept should be demonstrated with expected compile errors and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with expected compile errors and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Expected compile errors”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “Type-Level Testing”?
options: Assume testing exported api contracts is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check testing utility types, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.answer_key: Check testing utility types, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Testing utility types”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
